Is Psychology Today still worth it for therapists?

Ask this in any therapist group and you get the same two answers within an hour. One person gets most of their caseload from their profile and cannot imagine canceling. The next has paid for a year and heard from two people. Both are telling the truth. This is a guide to working out which one you are, written by a company that competes with Psychology Today, so read the last section with that in mind.

What therapists are actually reporting

The pattern in 2026 is a split, not a verdict. Therapists in less crowded areas, therapists who take insurance, and therapists with a clear specialty tend to report steady inquiries: two or three a month, sometimes four or five a week. Therapists in saturated metros, especially those who are private pay only or newly licensed, report one or two inquiries a year and a noticeable drop from the years before.

Two things make the drop feel worse than the raw numbers. First, an inquiry is not a client. The directory encourages people to contact several therapists at once, so a message often means you are one of three on a shortlist. Second, the searches that used to send people straight to a directory now also surface venture-funded platforms such as Headway, Alma, Grow and Rula, which take a share of each session. The pool of self-directed clients is the same size or smaller, and more companies are standing in front of it.

The math, done honestly

A listing runs about $30 a month, so roughly $360 a year. A single client who stays for ten sessions at $100 to $150 a session brings in $1,000 to $1,500. On that basis, one retained client a year pays for the listing several times over, which is the argument most therapists use to keep it.

Three corrections keep that argument honest:

  • Inquiries convert at well under 100%. If two people a year write to you and one becomes a client, the listing still pays. If two people write and neither does, it cost you $360 and some hope.
  • A tax deduction is not a refund. Writing the fee off reduces your taxable income by $360. Depending on your bracket, that gets you back roughly $70 to $130, not the whole fee.
  • Your time has a price. If staying visible means re-doing your profile every month, add those hours to the cost.

So the real question is not whether $360 is a lot. It is whether, in your area and your niche, the listing reliably produces at least one retained client a year, and whether anything cheaper would produce the same.

Signs it is still worth it for you

  • You can point to at least one client in the last twelve months who found you there and stayed.
  • You take insurance, or you practice in a town or county where the directory is thin.
  • Your profile is specific enough that a client can tell within two lines whether you are for them.
  • You use the listing for something else too: colleagues refer through it, or clients cite it as the place they checked your credentials.

Signs it is not

  • A year has passed with one or two inquiries and no retained client.
  • You practice in a saturated metro, private pay only, with a broad, general profile.
  • The inquiries you do get are people comparing three therapists, and you rarely hear back.
  • Most of your new clients already come from somewhere else: your own website, referrals, a former client's recommendation.

If three of those four describe you, canceling is a reasonable decision and not a failure. Keep the profile text somewhere; you may want it again if you move, add insurance, or narrow your niche.

If you stay, do what the busy ones do

The therapists who report steady inquiries describe a short, consistent list of habits. None of them is magic, and all of them take time.

  • Touch the profile monthly. A refreshed summary, new hours or a new photo appears to help a listing surface. Think of it as a recurring task, not a one-time setup.
  • Write to the client, not about yourself. Open with "you" rather than "I". Say what the person in front of you is probably feeling and what working together looks like.
  • Pick three things, not fifteen. A profile that claims every specialty reads as none. Three clear areas let a client recognize themselves.
  • Show your face and your room. A real photo of you, and one of the office if you see people in person, does more than any paragraph.
  • Finish everything, including the video. Incomplete profiles rank and convert worse.
  • If you only see clients by video, list a less crowded location in your state. You are licensed for the whole state, and the search is by city.
  • Answer within a day. The client who wrote to three therapists goes with the one who replied first and warmly.

What to run alongside it

Nobody should depend on one directory, and the therapists who are least anxious about any of them have two or three channels working at once.

  • Your own website with direct booking. The highest-trust channel there is, and the one nobody can raise the price on.
  • Colleague referrals. A short, specific note to five therapists you respect, saying exactly who you want referred, outperforms most paid listings.

Common questions

How much does a Psychology Today listing cost?

About $30 a month, which is roughly $360 a year. The fee is a business expense, so it reduces your taxable income, but a deduction gives back only a fraction of the fee, not the whole amount.

How many clients should I expect from Psychology Today?

It varies enormously by area, insurance and niche. Therapists in less crowded areas who take insurance often report two or three inquiries a month. Therapists in saturated cities who are private pay only often report one or two a year. An inquiry is not a client, since many people contact several therapists at once.

Should I cancel my Psychology Today profile?

If a full year has passed with one or two inquiries and no retained client, and most of your new clients already come from elsewhere, canceling is a reasonable decision. If you can point to a client in the last year who found you there and stayed, it is paying for itself. Keep a copy of your profile text either way.

Is Theraglee a replacement for Psychology Today?

It is a different kind of directory, and you do not have to cancel anything to try it. It is one flat rate with no per-session fees and every license is verified with the state board. It is also new, so the member community in your area may still be small.
